title: Why China is winning AI: competition in school and public rankings
summary: Durov argues China's AI catch-up (DeepSeek) stems from an education system that embraces competition and public rankings, borrowed from the Soviet model. Western schools that hide grades demotivate top students and mask the public rankings reality eventually imposes.

principles.text: Competition drives excellence; remove the losers and you remove the winners.
principles.quote: Victory and defeat are two sides of the same coin. Eliminate the losers — and you eliminate the winners

principles.text: Ambitious people are motivated by treating the game as a ranked contest against strong opponents.
principles.quote: For many students, motivation to excel in high school comes from treating it as a competitive game, striving to rank first against strong opponents.

principles.text: Transparency of performance matters: visible rankings make effort feel meaningful.
principles.quote: Removing transparency in student performance can make school feel meaningless for ambitious teenagers.

principles.text: Hiding rankings protects feelings but demotivates the best performers.
principles.quote: such measures also predictably demotivate the best students.

principles.text: Reality has public rankings in every field, so shielding people from them only delays the shock.
principles.quote: Reality, unlike well-meaning school policies, does have public grades and rankings — whether in sports, business, science, or technology.

principles.text: Public benchmarks are how competitive advantage becomes visible and decisive in tech.
principles.quote: AI benchmarks that demonstrate DeepSeek's superiority are one of such public rankings.
